english: Oh, I see / Ah, got it — a soft reaction when you just learned or understood something new.
usage: with 아 for a natural lead-in
reacting to a past event someone told you
examples: A: 나 사실 부산 출신이야 / B: 아, 그렇구나. 어쩐지 사투리가.
A: I'm actually from Busan / B: Oh I see. No wonder the accent.
reacting to new info from a friend
그렇구나. 그래서 어제 연락이 안 됐구나.
I see. So that's why I couldn't reach you yesterday.
piecing something together
A: 그 가게 월요일에 쉬어요 / B: 그렇군요. 알려주셔서 감사해요.
A: That shop is closed on Mondays / B: I see. Thanks for letting me know.
polite reply to a stranger
nuance: 그렇구나 (casual) and 그렇군요 (polite) are the natural 'oh, I see' you say when a fact clicks into place. It signals you took in what the other person said without strongly agreeing or judging, so it keeps a conversation flowing warmly. Use 그렇구나 with friends and 그렇군요 with people you keep -요 with; for past events switch to 그랬구나.
mistakes: Saying 그렇구나 to a boss or elder — it is casual banmal; use 그렇군요 or 그러시군요 instead

english: True / fair enough / come to think of it — used when you suddenly admit the other person has a point.
examples: A: 지금 가도 차 막혀서 똑같아 / B: 하긴, 그냥 천천히 가자.
A: Even if we leave now traffic's the same / B: Fair enough, let's just go slow.
conceding to a friend
하긴 너도 요즘 바빴으니까 이해해.
True, you've been busy lately too, so I get it.
softening, granting their side
A: 비 오는데 배달이 낫지 않아? / B: 하긴 그러네, 그냥 시키자.
A: It's raining, isn't delivery better? / B: Huh, you're right, let's just order.
changing your mind mid-talk
nuance: 하긴 is a casual filler that means 'now that you mention it, you're right' — a small concession after you reconsider. It often comes at the start of a reply, frequently as 하긴 그래 or 하긴 그러네, and feels relaxed and friendly. It is banmal-flavored, so among 20-30s friends it is everywhere, but in formal speech you would say 그건 그렇네요 or 맞는 말씀이에요 instead.
mistakes: Treating 하긴 as full agreement — it is a mild 'fair point,' not a strong yes; do not use it in formal settings

english: No wonder / that explains it — said when new info finally explains something you found odd.
usage: with 더라 for what you'd noticed
that's why it seemed that way
examples: A: 나 어제 밤새웠어 / B: 어쩐지 피곤해 보이더라.
A: I pulled an all-nighter / B: No wonder you looked tired.
explaining someone's state
문 닫았네. 어쩐지 불이 다 꺼져 있더라.
It's closed. No wonder all the lights were off.
realizing why something seemed off
A: 그 사람 사실 사장님 아들이래 / B: 어쩐지. 다들 조심하더라.
A: He's actually the boss's son / B: No wonder. Everyone was careful around him.
an explanation clicks
nuance: 어쩐지 is the 'no wonder / that explains it' reaction you use the moment a puzzle gets solved — you noticed something strange, and now you know why. It very often pairs with -더라 (어쩐지 …하더라) to recall what you had observed. It is conversational and works in both casual and softly polite speech; just add 요-level verbs around it for politeness.
mistakes: Confusing 어쩐지 (no wonder) with 어쨌든 (anyway) — they sound similar but mean different things

english: Anyway / by the way — used to change the subject or get back to what matters.
examples: 그래, 그것도 맞아. 그나저나 저녁 뭐 먹지?
Yeah, that's true too. Anyway, what should we eat for dinner?
pivoting to a real concern
그나저나 너 이사 준비는 잘 돼 가?
By the way, is your moving prep going okay?
bringing up something you care about
A: 그 얘긴 됐고 / B: 그나저나 주말에 시간 돼?
A: Enough about that / B: Anyway, are you free this weekend?
dropping a topic for a new one
nuance: 그나저나 means 'anyway / by the way' and is used to drop the current thread and bring up something you actually want to talk about. It feels casual and warm, like nudging the conversation toward what matters to you. It is fine in everyday polite talk too; in very formal settings you would prefer 그건 그렇고 or 다름이 아니라.
mistakes: Using 그나저나 in formal writing or business email — there use 그건 그렇고 or 한편

english: Anyway / in any case — used to wrap up or push past a tangent to the main point.
examples: 설명하자면 길어. 아무튼 결론은 못 가.
It's a long story. Anyway, the point is I can't go.
cutting to the conclusion
아무튼 도와줘서 진짜 고마워.
Anyway, thanks so much for the help.
wrapping up warmly
A: 그래서 어떻게 됐는데? / B: 아무튼 잘 끝났어.
A: So how did it turn out? / B: Anyway, it ended fine.
glossing over details
nuance: 아무튼 means 'anyway / regardless' and is used to brush past the details and land on what counts. Unlike 그나저나 (which switches to a new topic), 아무튼 wraps up the current one and drives to the point. It is everyday casual-to-polite; people sometimes say 아무튼 간에 for a touch more 'no matter what.'
mistakes: Mixing up 아무튼 (wrap up the current topic) with 그나저나 (switch to a new topic)

english: Anyway / either way / regardless — moves on while setting aside whatever was just said.
examples: 이유야 어쨌든, 결국 늦은 건 늦은 거야.
Whatever the reason, late is late in the end.
dismissing excuses
어쨌든 우리 둘 다 무사하니까 됐어.
Either way, we're both okay so it's fine.
focusing on the bottom line
A: 환불은 어렵다고 하던데 / B: 어쨌든 한번 문의는 해 봐.
A: They said a refund is hard / B: Either way, try asking once.
pushing forward regardless
nuance: 어쨌든 means 'either way / regardless' — you acknowledge what was said but treat it as not changing the outcome, then move on. It is close to 아무튼 but leans more on 'no matter what the case is.' It works in casual and polite speech alike; 어쨌거나 is a common interchangeable variant.
mistakes: Spelling it 어쨋든 — the correct spelling is 어쨌든

english: That's true, but… — agreeing partly while raising a 'but' or hesitation.
examples: A: 거기 싸고 좋잖아 / B: 그렇긴 한데 너무 멀어.
A: It's cheap and nice there / B: True, but it's too far.
agreeing then objecting
그렇긴 한데, 그래도 한 번 더 생각해 보자.
That's true, but still, let's think about it once more.
softening before pushing back
A: 운동 좀 해야 돼 / B: 그렇긴 해요. 시간이 없어서요.
A: You should work out / B: That's true. It's just I have no time.
polite half-agreement
nuance: 그렇긴 한데 means 'that's true, but…' — you grant the other person's point with 그렇긴, then the -ㄴ데 sets up your reservation. It is a gentle, face-saving way to disagree or hesitate without bluntly rejecting them. Casual; for polite speech say 그렇긴 한데요 or 그렇긴 해요 and continue your point.
mistakes: Spacing it as 그렇 긴 한데 — write 그렇긴 한데 (긴 attaches to 그렇)

english: Of course / absolutely — a warm, emphatic 'yes, definitely' in polite speech.
examples: A: 자리 좀 맡아 주실 수 있어요? / B: 그럼요, 앉으세요.
A: Could you save my seat? / B: Of course, have a seat.
agreeing warmly to a request
A: 내일도 문 열어요? / B: 그럼요, 평소대로 해요.
A: Are you open tomorrow too? / B: Of course, as usual.
shop staff reassuring
A: 이거 정말 가져가도 돼요? / B: 그럼요, 편하게 드세요.
A: Can I really take this? / B: Of course, help yourself.
offering generously
nuance: 그럼요 is a warm, confident 'of course / absolutely' that reassures the listener you fully agree or gladly say yes. The polite -요 makes it friendly with strangers, shop staff, and seniors, while plain 그럼 is the casual version for friends. It often pairs with 당연하죠 to sound extra welcoming.
mistakes: Confusing 그럼요 (of course) with 그럼 (in that case / well then) used as a transition word

english: Right? / I know / told you — sympathetic agreement, often with a hint of 'yeah, exactly.'
examples: A: 날씨 진짜 춥다 / B: 그러게, 갑자기 겨울 됐어.
A: It's so cold / B: I know, it suddenly turned winter.
agreeing with a friend
A: 진작 예약할걸 / B: 그러게, 자리가 없네.
A: We should've booked sooner / B: Right, there are no seats.
shared regret
A: 사람이 왜 이렇게 많아요 / B: 그러게요, 주말이라 그런가 봐요.
A: Why are there so many people / B: I know, must be because it's the weekend.
polite agreement with a stranger
nuance: 그러게 is a sympathetic 'right? / I know' that shows you feel exactly the same, often about something mildly annoying or regrettable. It can carry a soft 'told you so' when you predicted it. Use 그러게 with friends and 그러게요 with people you keep -요 with; 그러게 말이야 ramps up the agreement.
mistakes: Hearing 그러게 as a question — it is an agreeing reaction, not 'why did you do that'

english: Since you said so / because they were like that — explains why you acted, reacting to what someone said or did.
examples: 네가 먹고 싶다 그러길래 사 왔어.
You said you wanted some, so I bought it.
explaining why you did something
하도 맛있다고 그러길래 나도 시켜 봤어.
Everyone kept saying it's good, so I ordered it too.
reacting to repeated comments
A: 왜 먼저 갔어? / B: 다들 바쁘다 그러길래.
A: Why'd you leave first? / B: Everyone said they were busy, so…
justifying with a trailing reason
nuance: 그러길래 explains your own action as a reaction to what someone else said or did — 'since you/they were like that, I…'. It always points the cause at the other party, never at yourself, which separates it from plain 그래서. It is casual and conversational; the reason often trails off, leaving the result implied, as in 다들 바쁘다 그러길래.
mistakes: Using 그러길래 for your own reason — it must react to someone else's words or actions, unlike 그래서

english: I guess so / it seems so — a soft guess based on what you're seeing or hearing.
examples: 불이 꺼져 있네요. 오늘 쉬는 날인가 봐요.
The lights are off. I guess they're closed today.
inferring from a clue
A: 민수 씨 안 와요? / B: 연락이 없는 거 보니 그런가 봐요.
A: Isn't Minsu coming? / B: From the silence, I guess so.
guessing from evidence
A: 비 오려나 / B: 하늘 보니까 그런가 봐.
A: Is it going to rain / B: Looking at the sky, I guess so.
casual guess between friends
nuance: 그런가 봐요 means 'I guess so / it seems so' and is used to make a soft inference from something you observe rather than state a fact outright. The -나/은가 봐요 ending signals 'it looks like,' keeping you tentative and polite. Drop to 그런가 봐 with friends; flip to 아닌가 봐요 for 'I guess not.'
mistakes: Spacing as 그런가봐요 — standard spacing is 그런가 봐요 (봐요 is a separate auxiliary)

english: Now that you mention it / hearing you say that — you reconsider after listening to someone.
examples: 듣고 보니 네 말이 맞는 것 같아.
Now that you mention it, I think you're right.
coming around to their view
A: 이 색이 너한테 더 어울려 / B: 듣고 보니 그러네.
A: This color suits you better / B: Now that you say it, yeah.
agreeing after reconsidering
듣고 보니까 그 식당 좀 비싸긴 했어.
Come to think of it, that restaurant was kind of pricey.
recalling after the topic comes up
nuance: 듣고 보니 literally means 'having heard and looked,' and it works as 'now that you mention it' — you take in what someone said and reconsider, usually ending up agreeing. It often leads into 그렇네 or 맞네 to show your mind changed. It is natural in both casual and polite speech; add -까 (듣고 보니까) before a longer follow-up clause.
mistakes: Reading it literally as 'after listening' only — in conversation it signals you've reconsidered and tend to agree
